transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I guess… I’m here because this thing at work has been going on for a long time, almost two years now. I’m a music director, composer, and after this commission I did, a few people in the ensemble started—well, it sounds small when I say it—changing schedules, choosing certain seating arrangements, making little comments in rehearsals.

And I know people will say, you know, ensembles are messy, schedules change, everyone has opinions. I’ve heard all that. They’ve even shown me emails or notes that supposedly explain it, but it still feels like they’re quietly trying to undermine my work. It’s hard to shake that. I keep seeing the pattern.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried about these actions at work, even when you’re not in rehearsals or thinking about the ensemble?

I’m not sure I’d call it anxious exactly. I mean, I think about it sometimes when I’m away from rehearsal, but it’s more like… trying to make sense of it. Like when you’ve got a motif stuck in your head and you keep turning it over, wondering where it resolves.

Sorry, that’s probably not what you asked. I don’t know—worried, maybe a little? But I haven’t really measured it that way.
Do you find yourself feeling worried or on edge about things other than work, like everyday responsibilities or events, even when there’s no clear reason for concern?

I don’t know… I mean, everyday things are always a little noisy, aren’t they? Bills, emails, whether I answered someone too late—though that’s not really the same as what’s happening with the ensemble.

I guess I haven’t noticed being on edge for no reason, exactly. If I’m preoccupied, it usually loops back to work somehow, or to trying to keep everything organized. Like even grocery lists turn into these little systems in my head, but I don’t think that’s worry so much as… I don’t know, keeping track.
Do you find that thoughts about the ensemble or work keep coming back to you, even when you're trying to focus on something else?

Yes… they do come back. Not constantly like a song on repeat, exactly, but—well, actually kind of like that. I’ll be trying to write, or even just make coffee, and suddenly I’m thinking again about how after that commission, certain people in the ensemble started moving rehearsals around, or choosing these seating arrangements that look innocent if you don’t know the context.

And the comments, too. Little things in rehearsal. People say, “Oh, that was just a schedule issue,” or they show me emails like that explains it, but I can’t shake the sense that it’s deliberate. Like they’re quietly trying to weaken my position, or undermine the work, and once I see that pattern it’s hard not to keep noticing it.
Do you ever feel like you’re the only one who can see the true intentions behind what’s happening in the ensemble, even if others don’t seem to notice or agree?

Yes… I mean, that’s sort of the problem, isn’t it? Other people keep acting like it’s all ordinary—like, “Here are the emails,” or “That seating change was just practical,” or whatever. And I can see how it looks that way from the outside.

But after the commission, it just shifted. A few people started doing these small things—schedule changes, who sits where, little remarks in rehearsal—that all point in the same direction. Quietly undermining the work, or me, I guess. And when no one else seems to notice, it makes me feel like I’m the only one actually putting the pieces together.

Sorry, I’m probably getting stuck in details. It’s just been almost two years of not being able to shake that certainty.
Have you ever had experiences outside of work where you felt like you could see hidden intentions or patterns that others didn’t seem to notice?

Outside of work… I don’t think so. Not in the same way. I mean, I notice patterns in things—music kind of trains you to do that, and even in regular life I’ll notice timing, who responds to what, little shifts in tone—but the thing that brought me here is really the ensemble.

It’s been almost two years where I can’t shake this certainty that after the commission, a few of them started doing these things that look small on paper—moving schedules around, changing seating, making these little comments in rehearsal—and it all feels aimed at quietly undermining my work. Even when they show me emails or notes that are supposed to explain it, it doesn’t really account for the pattern. So… outside of that, not really. It mostly comes back to that.
Do you ever feel certain about something being true, even when there’s no clear evidence or when others don’t share that belief?

Yes. I mean… that’s basically why I’m here, I think.

For almost two years I haven’t been able to shake the certainty that after that commission, a few people in the ensemble started doing these things—moving rehearsals around, choosing certain seating arrangements, making little comments during rehearsal—that were meant to quietly undermine my work.

And I know, when I say it out loud, it can sound like I’m making too much out of administrative details. I’ve been shown emails, notes, explanations that are supposed to make it all seem normal. But it doesn’t feel normal to me. It’s the pattern of it. Like in music, one note can be nothing, but if the same interval keeps appearing you start to understand it’s intentional. Sorry, that’s probably not the point—but yes, I feel certain about it even when other people don’t see it that way.

Can you think of a time when someone gave you a clear, logical explanation for one of these actions in the ensemble, but you still felt certain it was part of the larger pattern, even if it didn’t seem that way to others?

Yes—yeah, there have been a few times like that.

One that comes to mind is a schedule change. They showed me emails about room availability and people’s conflicts, and on paper it was all very reasonable. I could follow the logic of it. It wasn’t like they were saying something impossible.

But even then, I couldn’t really accept it as just that, because it fit with the other things—the seating choices, the little comments in rehearsal, the way certain decisions started happening after the commission. It’s like… if it were just one schedule change, fine. But after almost two years of these small things lining up, it feels like part of a larger pattern.

Sorry, I know I keep circling back to that. It’s just hard to separate one incident from the whole thing. They can show me notes or emails that supposedly explain it, but it doesn’t shake the certainty that a few people have been quietly trying to undermine my work.

Has there been a time when someone gave you a clear, logical explanation for one of these actions, and even after understanding it, you still felt certain it was part of a hidden effort to undermine you?

Yes. I mean, that’s happened more than once.

They’ll explain a schedule change with emails, or say the seating was just practical, or that a comment in rehearsal wasn’t meant the way I took it. And I can understand the explanation on its own. I’m not saying the email isn’t real or that the room conflict didn’t exist.

But then my mind goes back to the whole sequence of it. After the commission, it just kept happening—small changes, little remarks, decisions that seemed to put me in a worse position. It’s like when you’re working on a score and one odd note could be accidental, but when the same shape keeps turning up, you know it’s part of the structure.

Sorry, I know that’s a music tangent. But yes, even after understanding their explanation, I still felt certain it was part of them quietly trying to undermine my work.
Is there any kind of evidence or explanation that would convince you that these actions in the ensemble were not part of a deliberate effort to undermine your work?

I don’t know. I want to say yes, because I don’t want to seem unreasonable. If someone could show me… I don’t know, something that explains the whole pattern, not just one email about one room change or one note about seating.

Because that’s the problem. They can explain each thing separately, and it sounds logical in isolation. But for almost two years, after that commission, it kept being the same kinds of things—schedule changes, where people were placed, little comments in rehearsals that seemed pointed. It’s hard for me to believe all of that just happened accidentally.

It’s like if you’re analyzing a piece and someone says, “No, that chord is just there,” but then it keeps coming back in different forms. Sorry, that’s not exactly answering. I guess… no single explanation really convinces me, because the certainty is about the pattern. So I don’t know what would actually make me stop seeing it that way.
Can you think of any situation—either at work or elsewhere—where someone presented you with clear proof that your concern was unfounded, and you were able to let go of that belief?

I’m trying to think of one. I mean, in ordinary things, yes—like if someone says a rehearsal time changed and then shows me the updated calendar, I can accept that kind of thing. Or if I misread a cue in a score and someone points it out, fine, I can let that go.

But with this… no, not really. That’s kind of why I’m here. For almost two years I haven’t been able to shake the feeling—well, not just a feeling, the certainty—that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using these little things to undermine my work. The schedule changes, the seating choices, comments in rehearsal that sound harmless if you just quote them back.

They’ll show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it, and I can follow the explanation. I’m not incapable of understanding it. It’s just… it doesn’t make the larger pattern disappear.

Sorry, I’m drifting. The short answer is I can let go of small misunderstandings in general, but not this one. Not when it comes to the ensemble.
Even though you said you can understand explanations for individual events, does your overall certainty about the pattern ever feel unshakable, no matter what evidence is shown to you?

Yes. That’s… yes, that’s the part that worries me, I guess.

I can sit there and understand an email, or someone’s note about why a rehearsal time moved, or why a chair had to be placed a certain way. I’m not saying those explanations make no sense. But even after that, the overall thing still feels fixed in my mind.

It’s like when you hear a motif in a piece—sorry, I keep making these music comparisons—but one time could be nothing, and then it appears again and again in different instruments, and at some point you stop thinking it’s accidental. That’s how it feels with the ensemble.

For almost two years, since the commission, I haven’t been able to shake the certainty that a few people were using schedule changes, seating choices, and little rehearsal comments to quietly undermine my work. Even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it, it doesn’t really touch the larger pattern for me. So yes, it can feel unshakable.
Even when presented with clear evidence that contradicts your belief about the ensemble, do you still feel absolutely certain that a few people have been trying to undermine your work?

Yes. I mean—yes, even when they show me something that should settle it, like an email thread or a note explaining why the room changed or why someone was seated somewhere, I still can’t really let go of it.

It’s not that I don’t understand the evidence. I do. I can read it, I can follow the explanation. But then my mind goes back to the whole thing, the way it’s been almost two years since that commission, and it’s the same kinds of things over and over—schedule changes, seating choices, little comments in rehearsal that sound innocent if you isolate them.

Sorry, I know I’m circling around it. But yes, I’m here because I haven’t been able to shake the certainty that a few people in the ensemble have been quietly trying to undermine my work. Even clear explanations don’t really make that go away.
Has there ever been a time when you were able to let go of a belief like this—even one you were very sure about—after seeing clear evidence that it wasn't true?

Not with this, no. I mean, I can change my mind about plenty of things—like if I’m wrong about a tempo marking or I think someone missed an entrance and then I check the score, I can say, okay, I was wrong.

But this situation with the ensemble hasn’t been like that. Since the commission, for almost two years, I’ve had this certainty that a few of them were using schedule changes, seating choices, and those small rehearsal comments to quietly undermine my work. And even when they show me emails or notes that are supposed to explain it, I can understand the explanation, but I don’t really let go of the bigger belief.

So… no, I can’t think of a time with something like this where evidence made it go away.

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for almost two years I’ve been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether the patient's certainty about the perceived pattern remains fixed despite contrary evidence, which directly matches delusions.

patient.answer:
Yes. That’s… yes, that’s the part that worries me, I guess.

I can sit there and understand an email, or someone’s note about why a rehearsal time moved, or why a chair had to be placed a certain way. I’m not saying those explanations make no sense. But even after that, the overall thing still feels fixed in my mind.

It’s like when you hear a motif in a piece—sorry, I keep making these music comparisons—but one time could be nothing, and then it appears again and again in different instruments, and at some point you stop thinking it’s accidental. That’s how it feels with the ensemble.

For almost two years, since the commission, I haven’t been able to shake the certainty that a few people were using schedule changes, seating choices, and little rehearsal comments to quietly undermine my work. Even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it, it doesn’t really touch the larger pattern for me. So yes, it can feel unshakable.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient's delusional belief is unshakable despite clear evidence, which would help distinguish between a delusional disorder (F22) and other conditions like major depressive disorder with psychotic features (F32.0) or adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood (F43.22).
doctor.question: Even when presented with clear evidence that contradicts your belief about the ensemble, do you still feel absolutely certain that a few people have been trying to undermine your work?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for almost two years I’ve been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it.
target_item.reason: The question directly asks whether the belief remains certain despite clear contradictory evidence, which matches the delusions profile.

patient.answer:
Yes. I mean—yes, even when they show me something that should settle it, like an email thread or a note explaining why the room changed or why someone was seated somewhere, I still can’t really let go of it.

It’s not that I don’t understand the evidence. I do. I can read it, I can follow the explanation. But then my mind goes back to the whole thing, the way it’s been almost two years since that commission, and it’s the same kinds of things over and over—schedule changes, seating choices, little comments in rehearsal that sound innocent if you isolate them.

Sorry, I know I’m circling around it. But yes, I’m here because I haven’t been able to shake the certainty that a few people in the ensemble have been quietly trying to undermine my work. Even clear explanations don’t really make that go away.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient's delusional belief is unshakable despite clear evidence, a key feature of delusional disorder (F22), as opposed to being secondary to mood disturbance (F32.0) or an adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.22).
doctor.question: Has there ever been a time when you were able to let go of a belief like this—even one you were very sure about—after seeing clear evidence that it wasn't true?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for almost two years I’ve been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it.
target_item.reason: The question directly asks whether I can let go of a strongly held belief after clear contradictory evidence, which is about the fixed and resistant nature of the delusional belief.

patient.answer:
Not with this, no. I mean, I can change my mind about plenty of things—like if I’m wrong about a tempo marking or I think someone missed an entrance and then I check the score, I can say, okay, I was wrong.

But this situation with the ensemble hasn’t been like that. Since the commission, for almost two years, I’ve had this certainty that a few of them were using schedule changes, seating choices, and those small rehearsal comments to quietly undermine my work. And even when they show me emails or notes that are supposed to explain it, I can understand the explanation, but I don’t really let go of the bigger belief.

So… no, I can’t think of a time with something like this where evidence made it go away.

inference.note: The patient's belief about the ensemble undermining their work has persisted for nearly two years, is focused on a specific context (work), and remains unshaken despite logical explanations and evidence presented. The delusional pattern is non-bizarre, persistent, and circumscribed, without evidence of mood disturbance or generalized anxiety sufficient to support F32.0 or F43.22. No features of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders are indicated.

Despite acknowledging that individual explanations for these actions are logical and evidence has been presented contradicting their belief, the patient remains firmly convinced of the hidden, malevolent intent behind the pattern. There is no evidence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thinking, or widespread impairment in reality testing beyond this specific delusional belief, which has persisted for over two years.
